schools.summary: Ellicott frames the trouble as Jews wronging Jews; Keil and Delitzsch set the outcry during the wall-building, the poor crushed by the burden and by wealthy usurers until discontent broke into loud complaint.

Henry reads the tears of the oppressed (Eccl. 4:1), the governor's charge to deliver the poor (Ps. 82:4), a dearth sent for neglected worship (Haggai 1:9; Mal. 3:9), and the aggravation of oppressors lately freed themselves (Isa. 58:6).
Gill hears in the great cry the voice of the poorer sort.

themes: the governor's duty to the oppressed

schools.summary: Gill: a numerous offspring was a blessing, but a large household needed much food.
Keil and Delitzsch identify the landless labourers asking (not seizing) that corn be furnished; Ellicott reads the words as a general appeal for the governor's help.
Clarke hears families too large to provide for, driven into debt; Wesley marks the paradox that many children, a blessing, was turned to a curse on unreasonable terms.
Henry: the most necessitous families were the most numerous — the mouths were there, but where was the meat? — and those with abundance must supply the wants of others (Ezek. 16:49).

themes: children a blessing turned to burden
the duty of the full toward the hungry

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch read the participle as an accomplished, continuing mortgage — 'we have been obliged to pledge them' — and ask corn because the lands are already pawned; Ellicott takes the 'dearth' as present hunger, not a formal famine.
Clarke recalls the judicial drought of Haggai 1:9 but leans to a fresh scarcity from swollen numbers; Wesley traces the shortage to the crowd, the building work, and the fear of invasion.
Gill: they had made their fields, vineyards, and houses over as pledges for money.

debates.question: What was the 'dearth' that drove them to mortgage?

sides.position: A real scarcity — a lingering or renewed judicial drought, or a famine from swollen numbers
Not a formal famine at all, but simply their present hunger, resources already straitened by the mortgages

themes: corn sought against a pledged harvest

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch explain the pledging of the crops to raise the tribute money (Lev. 25:14); Ellicott: the fields made answerable for the Persian tribute, the coming produce pledged.
Clarke names the tribute a token of subjection to Persia, not heavy in itself but beyond the impoverished returnees' means.
Gill notes some speakers could buy corn without mortgaging, yet were crushed by the tribute all the same.
Henry: high taxes atop dear corn, a poll-money perhaps, so the largest households paid the most — the mark of captivity still upon them.

themes: a levy heaviest on large families

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch: one flesh with the rich, yet unrelieved by the law (Deut. 15:7) and forced to enslave sons and daughters they cannot redeem; Ellicott calls the bondage of the children the climax of the cry.
Clarke cites the law permitting sale of children in necessity (Exod. 21:7); Wesley marks that even the tender daughters were sold, proof of extreme need, with no means to redeem.
Henry gives the plea its voice — children as dear and as free-born as the rulers' own, sealed with circumcision (Mal. 2:10; Job 31:15), yet their heirs made slaves beyond redemption.
Gill: same nature, nation, stock, and religion, entitled to the same privileges.

themes: sons and daughters sold to bondage

schools.summary: Henry commends anger that serves reform — Nehemiah would not shelve a just complaint though the work pressed, for no wall keeps a city safe while such abuses stand; it well becomes rulers to be angry at sin, yet governed anger, unlike Ezra's tender grief.
Gill: the cry stirred both compassion for the poor and indignation at the rich.
Keil and Delitzsch mark the anger at the injustice as the opening of the abolition of usury; Ellicott notes Nehemiah, newly arrived, had not known this hidden state of things.

themes: a just complaint heard at once

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch: 'my heart took counsel' (Dan. 4:24), the sin lying in the burdensome pledge (Deut. 24:10), not lending as such; Ellicott has Nehemiah master himself, the offenders breaking the law's spirit, and reads a general assembly 'concerning' not 'against' them.

Clarke: usury against God's law and doubly cruel, perhaps near a Sabbatical year (Deut. 15:2); Wesley cites the plain prohibition (Deut. 23:19) and the assembly of the mostly guiltless as impartial judges.
Gill: Nehemiah consulting what method to take to redress the grievance.
Henry: reproofs must be given with consideration, and no man's dignity sets him above reproof.

outliers.note: Renders the last clause not that Nehemiah set the assembly 'against them' but that he called a general assembly 'concerning them.'

themes: rebuke of the nobles and rulers

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch fix 'after our ability' (as far as we were able) and the antithesis of buying back against selling; Ellicott: they redeemed Jews from the heathen while these sold Jews to Jews — an argument that shamed them to silence.

Henry drives it home: a people redeemed from the heathen at great cost, some ransomed by Nehemiah himself, now re-enslaved by their own rulers — the freed brought again under a yoke (Gal. 5:1; 1 Cor. 7:23).
Gill: the words addressed to the nobles, rulers, and rich exacters of usury.

Keil and Delitzsch: walk in the fear of God so as not to give the enemies occasion to reproach; Ellicott sets the watchful heathen of Nehemiah 6 who would turn every oppression into a reproach against God.
Clarke: abstain from cruelty in the heathen's sight or they will not credit a God-given religion; Wesley: the enemies round about observe all and will reproach both people and faith.
Henry: those who fear God dare not do a wicked thing (Job 31:13), and nothing exposes religion to reproach more than the hard-heartedness of its professors.
Gill reads 'not good' as a meiosis — meaning it was very bad.

themes: walk in the fear of God

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch: 'we are those who have lent' — the appeal is to remit, not to demand back, the loan; Ellicott: by his own example the governor pleads, 'let us remit the loans,' putting himself first.
Wesley: his brethren in office and servants might have exacted a just recompense, but he freely remits his own right, laying no burden he will not share.
Gill: he too might justly have exacted, but declines for the sake of easing the poor.
Henry: those who rigorously insist on their own right will ill persuade others to recede from theirs.

outliers.note: Insist Nehemiah asks not that creditors refund interest already taken, but that they remit what is still owing and loose the pledges they still hold.

themes: let us leave off this usury

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch: restore the pledged lands this very day and remit the interest still owing (not refund interest received); Ellicott reads the 'hundredth part' as the one-percent monthly, twelve percent yearly, to be given up.

Wesley takes the hundredth part as the monthly interest to be no longer required; Clarke, following Houbigant, denies the word means a hundredth at all — the versions acknowledge none — reading 'a part from the money,' though allowing the twelve-percent sense.
Gill urges immediate restitution, noting Aben Ezra's view that it was the year of release.
Henry: he beseeches rather than commands — restore the estates, remit the interest, give time for the principal — for what we charitably forgive shall be recompensed.

debates.question: What is 'the hundredth part' Nehemiah bids them restore?

sides.position: The one-percent monthly interest (twelve percent a year) to be given up henceforth
Not a hundredth at all, but 'a part from the money' — the versions acknowledge no hundredth part (Houbigant)

schools.summary: Ellicott: the promise to restore and require no more interest, sealed by an oath for legal validity and by the priests' presence for religious sanction; Keil and Delitzsch confirm the promise, the priests, and the oath.
Henry lays out the ascending obligations — promise, then oath before the priests while conviction was fresh, then curse — unlike Jeremiah's men who re-enslaved those they had freed (Jer. 34:10).
Wesley: the oath taken before the priests, who act in God's name, to make the deeper impression on the conscience.
Gill notes the ready promise to restore the lands and require nothing more.
Keil and Delitzsch read the shaken lap as a symbolical act to bind the oath; Ellicott presses the imprecation — emptied as the fold is emptied — and notes the sin never recurs (Neh. 10; Neh. 13).
Clarke likens it to the Roman envoys who shook out the toga to declare war on Carthage (Livy).
Henry: the people's Amen, as at Ebal (Deut. 27), their praise, and the performance that followed — good promises, but good performances all in all.
Gill: he shook the fore-skirts, letting the dust fall, as a symbol of the curse.

themes: so may God shake out the covenant-breaker

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch make the transaction the occasion of Nehemiah's larger testimony of unselfishness; Ellicott dates the passage after his return, on review of his twelve-year governorship in the land of Judah.

Clarke details the governor's due — bread, wine, and forty shekels a day — which Nehemiah never took; Wesley: he governed twelve years, present or by deputy, forgoing the allowance the law and the king allowed.
Henry: he tells his practice not in pride but to move his successors to tenderness — he did the governor's work but ate not the governor's bread, the bondage being heavy on the people.
Gill dates the appointment by Artaxerxes after the wall was finished, the twelve years running to the thirty-second year.

Keil and Delitzsch: the former governors burdened the people with bread, wine, and forty shekels, their servants bearing rule; Ellicott reckons some four pounds a day, a satrap's practice, against the interdict with its 'Fear thy God' (Lev. 25:36; 25:43).
Wesley: not Ezra nor Zerubbabel but unnamed successors, whose servants' cruelty is charged upon the masters.
Gill: the governors between Zerubbabel and Nehemiah, Ezra being no governor.
Henry: Nehemiah spares their names to their honour; only the fear of God, for conscience' sake, restrained him where they had preyed.

debates.question: Whom does Nehemiah mean by the 'former governors' he censures?

sides.position: Unnamed successors of Zerubbabel — not Zerubbabel himself, nor Ezra who held no such office
Zerubbabel together with his successors, all of whom received the allowances and burdened the people

themes: restrained by the fear of God

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch: he set his hand to the wall and bought no land — took no mortgages of the poor — his servants gathered to the work; Ellicott reads 'I continued' as 'I repaired,' the household absorbed in the common labour.
Clarke: neither he nor his officers bought the people's land, and he set his servants to the wall; Wesley: the poor's necessities offered good bargains he refused.
Henry: not a bad husband but a good governor who feathered no nest — it is more blessed to give than receive (Acts 20:35) — and his servants too were set to the work.
Gill: he gave constant attendance to direct and encourage the workmen.

themes: buying no land of the poor

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch identify the hundred and fifty as the heads of the houses of Judah (Neh. 2:16), always his guests with visiting Jews; Ellicott weighs the heavy charge of the governor's free hospitality.
Clarke: an open house met from savings made as the king's cup-bearer at Susa; Wesley: rulers as well as commoners, resorting to give notice of the enemies' designs and receive orders.
Henry: a constant good table for persons of the first rank — those in public place are preferred to do good, and all should use hospitality without grudging (1 Pet. 4:9).
Gill: a hundred and fifty daily at his own considerable cost.

themes: a hundred and fifty at his table
open hospitality at his own cost
the table as seat of government
preferred to do good, not to enrich

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch itemize the daily ox, six choice sheep, fowls, and wine every ten days, yet the governor's bread refused because the service lay heavy on the people.

Clarke reckons food for over two hundred, offers two readings of the ten-day wine, and compares the bey of Tunis; Wesley: borne from his own considerable estate, his court office a place of great profit.
Henry: he would not demand the governor's bread though it cost his own estate, for in our demands we must weigh not only their justice but the ability of those on whom we make them.
Gill notes the ox and six fat sheep, evidence of how good a table he kept.

outliers.note: Offers two readings of 'once in ten days store of all sorts of wine' — either they drank wine only every tenth day, or the servants restocked wine every ten days.

themes: one ox and six choice sheep

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch render the plain petition, repeated in Nehemiah 13:14, a man leaving his reward with God; Ellicott marks the modesty that seeks recompense from God, not the people, far from any fame of his deeds.
Clarke: he offers no good deeds to extenuate sin but asks mercy as he showed mercy ('Forgive, and ye shall be forgiven'); Wesley: as I did thy people good for thy sake, do me good for thine own.
Henry: he mentions his deeds not in pride but to shame the rulers, and prays not as claiming a debt but as depending on God alone, reckoning God's favour reward enough (Ps. 40:5).
Gill: he looks for recompense not from the people but from the Lord, and that of grace, not merit.

themes: think upon me, my God, for good
reward sought from God, not men
